they intersect at a finite number of points but greater than
\(2\)

flags: The notation log2x is read conventionally as log(2x).
The expression log2x is interpreted as log(2x), with both logarithms having the same fixed base greater than zero and unequal to one.

question: Consider the graphs of \(y=2\log x\) and \(y=\log2x.\) We may say that:
solution:
Read \(\log2x\) conventionally as \(\log(2x)\), with both logarithms having the same fixed base \(a>0\), \(a\ne1\). Both graphs have domain \(x>0\).

An intersection occurs exactly when the two functions give the same value at the same \(x\). Using the logarithm product rule, this condition becomes
\[
2\log_a x=\log_a(2x)
=\log_a2+\log_a x.
\]
Subtracting \(\log_a x\) gives
\[
\log_a x=\log_a2.
\]
A logarithmic function is strictly increasing when \(a>1\) and strictly decreasing when \(0<a<1\), so equal logarithms have equal arguments. Therefore \(x=2\) is the only possible intersection abscissa.

At \(x=2\), both functions equal \(2\log_a2=\log_a4\), so this intersection does exist. Hence there is exactly one intersection, choice B.
